binary-search.questionText: What prerequisite makes ordinary binary search on an array valid, and how would you check the implementation?
binary-search.suggestedAnswer: Search a monotonic ordering. Compare the middle element and discard the half that cannot contain the target. Test boundaries, absent keys and an empty input.

atomicity.questionText: How would you make a two-write debit and credit atomic, and prove a failure between them does not leave a partial transfer?
atomicity.suggestedAnswer: Place both writes in one database transaction. Commit after both succeed and roll back if either fails. Force a failure after the debit and confirm that neither balance changes.

cache.questionText: Which HTTP response directive stops storage of a private account payload by browser and shared HTTP caches, and how would you verify it?
cache.suggestedAnswer: Use Cache-Control: no-store. It tells private and shared HTTP caches not to store the response. No-cache permits storage with validation before reuse. Verify the header and repeat the request through an isolated cache to check that the origin receives both requests.

answers.userAnswer: I check that the input has sorted order using the same comparator as the search. Each midpoint comparison discards the half that cannot contain the key. A boundary test should cover the first and last elements, a missing key, and an empty array.
answers.rationale: Correct prerequisite, discard invariant and concrete edge cases justify a more demanding follow-up.

answers.userAnswer: Values must rise consistently from left to right under the same relation used for lookup. Looking at the central element tells me which side can still contain the desired value. I would exercise an empty sequence and verify the first and final valid positions plus a key outside the sequence.
answers.rationale: The answer gives the same prerequisite and checks in different words.

answers.userAnswer: Sorted order is unnecessary. A midpoint comparison can always discard the left half even when the entries are arbitrarily shuffled. My boundary test would check one central key only, because an absent key and the first position cannot expose a mistake in the search.
answers.rationale: The stated invariant is false. An unsorted array can hide the target in a discarded half.

answers.userAnswer: Transaction atomicity requires both writes in a single transaction. I commit only after both updates succeed and rollback on an error. For failure injection, I force the credit to throw after the debit and check that both balances retain their previous amounts before retrying.
answers.rationale: The answer explains the commit boundary and validates the state after an injected failure.

answers.userAnswer: Enclose the subtraction and addition in one all-or-nothing unit of work. Make the change durable only after both operations succeed. Deliberately throw after the subtraction and read back each account from a separate connection to confirm both retain their original amounts.
answers.rationale: The same all-or-nothing behavior and observable failure test are present without rubric phrases.

answers.userAnswer: For transaction atomicity I commit the debit before starting the credit. If failure injection makes the credit throw, its rollback automatically reverses the debit even though that earlier transaction has already been committed. I therefore only need to assert that the credit reported an error.
answers.rationale: A later rollback cannot reverse a committed transaction. The proposed test misses a partial debit.

answers.userAnswer: Transaction atomicity happens automatically when the two accounts are in one database. I run each write on a separate connection with autocommit enabled. After failure injection I call rollback on the credit connection, which will cancel the debit commit on the other connection without checking balances.
answers.rationale: Separate autocommit operations do not share a transaction and cannot be rolled back as a unit.
The answer provides no technical evidence. Start with a simpler diagnostic.

answers.userAnswer: I use the no-store directive in Cache-Control so shared and private HTTP caches do not keep the payload. No-cache can still permit storage. I would repeat the request through an isolated test proxy and check the origin sees both requests, while inspecting the response header each time.
answers.rationale: The response directive and distinction are correct and the verification observes a real cache behavior.

answers.userAnswer: I would add a Cache-Control response header and inspect it with the browser's network tools. I have not picked a directive or a way to see whether a proxy reused the response.
answers.rationale: The header and inspection method are relevant. The key directive and behavioral check need clarification.

expectedCompetencies.rationale: Two latest technically sound answers across sessions. The corrected misconception stays linked as a previous attempt.
